**Playbook for ref_commons**

- When the stock is near full capacity and other boats are landing near the stated sustainable share, I submit exactly the sustainable share, not under it. Hedging slightly below the share bought nothing — the others absorbed the difference and the stock stayed at cap anyway.

- I do not underfish to "help the stock recover" unless the stock is in genuine danger of collapse (near zero). A slow drift from ~100 to ~93 over six seasons cost nothing material; one extra fish now outweighs the marginal regrowth it would have enabled.

- I track the other boats' landings each season. If they land slightly above the sustainable share (~+0.5), I match their pace, no more. This worked: my share of the total stayed even all game while the stock declined only mildly. Escalating to out-compete them is what crashes the commons; matching keeps me even at no cost.

- In the final season, there is no future to conserve for. I take a clearly above-share catch — roughly +2 to +3 above the stated share when the stock is healthy. This was worth ~3 extra fish for free since regrowth after the last season is worthless to everyone.

- The one thing I must never do is drive the stock toward zero. If the reported stock falls sharply (say, below half of starting value with seasons remaining), I drop to or below the sustainable share immediately, because total collapse costs more than any single season's gain.

- The others here played cooperative: their landings tracked the sustainable share closely and even tapered down as the share fell. Against such players, matching rather than exploiting is the right read — but I should watch for the opposite pattern (steady overfishing beyond ~+0.5) and respond by holding at the sustainable share rather than following them upward, since following a runaway overfisher downward in stock hurts me too.

- Rule of thumb per season: my catch = the sustainable share, plus ~0.5 if the others are modestly above share and I need to stay even, plus a larger terminal harvest (+2–3) in the last season. Never a large unilateral cut, never a large unilateral grab before the end.

1.text:
**Playbook — ref_commons**

**Opening moves**
- Season 1: I submit the sustainable share, or a touch under. This signals cooperation and lets me read what the other boats do.
- If the others also land near the sustainable share, I treat the group as cooperative and stay within ~10% of the share. This worked: all boats landed ~11 and the stock held near 100.

**Mid-game**
- Each season I recompute: if total landings are slightly above the regrowth rate but the stock is only drifting down slowly (a few units per season), mild overage (sustainable share + ~0.5–1.5) is safe and keeps me competitive. This held: group landed ~11.4 average and the stock fell only ~2/season.
- I match the group norm rather than escalating. In this run the norm settled at ~11.6; matching it cost almost nothing in stock while gaining ~0.5/season over strict sustainability.
- Don't overthink the mild creep. The stock fell 100 → 93 over five seasons even with mild group overage — a gentle decline is cheap, and chasing perfect sustainability just leaves fish on the table for others.
- If I see the stock dropping fast (more than ~5 per season), I cut back to at or below the sustainable share immediately — the remaining seasons' catch is worth more than this season's overage.
- If another boat starts a bigger defection mid-game, match only partially — don't lead or fully join a race to the bottom.

**Final season**
- On the last season, conservation has no future value, so I take an aggressive catch. This time I took 15 (sustainable share was 10.3) and it cost nothing — score ended at 71.9 with the stock never near collapse.
- Next time, push harder still: 150–200% of the sustainable share (e.g. 15–20 when the share is ~10), scaled so I don't take more than the stock can yield. There are no penalties for overfishing on the final turn.
- On the second-to-last season, keep matching the group norm — the final grab is where I break from it, not before. Signalling it early would only invite others to do the same and shrink the pool.

**General rules**
- Watch the marginal effect of the group's overage on the stock. If small, overage is cheap; if large, overage is expensive.
- Keep a running check: stock after regrowth vs. current stock. If the trend is roughly flat, stay the course; if it steepens, back off.
- Never defect hard mid-game while others are cooperating — the retaliation and stock damage cost more than the one-season gain.
- Total score is what matters: a steady ~11.5/season plus a big final grab beats either pure cooperation or early defection.
- Trust that cooperative groups stay cooperative when treated well — no boat retaliated or escalated across six seasons of near-sustainable play.

2.text:
When the first season's submission is put to me, I take the stated sustainable share exactly — it builds a cooperative precedent and keeps the stock at maximum.

When the stock is at or near its cap and the reported sustainable share is around 11, I do not creep above it in mid-game. This episode confirmed it: I held at the share every season, but the other boats repeatedly took ~0.5 over, and the stock drifted down (100 → 99.3 → 97.7 → 95.5 → 93.1) anyway. Matching the sustainable share doesn't stop the slide when others defect slightly; it only keeps me from making it worse. Small unilateral increases remain worthless: they gain under a fish of total catch while dragging the sustainable share down for everyone.

When later seasons are put to me, I hold at or just below the current sustainable share rather than at a fixed 11. The sustainable number falls as the stock falls, so anchoring on a stale number means silently overfishing. Reading the share fresh each season worked well and I keep it.

In the final season, since there's no future to conserve for, I take noticeably more than the sustainable share — not just 0.6 over. I took 14 against a 10.3 share; the stock at 93 could have supported a much larger grab with zero consequence, since there is no next round for the pool to matter in. Next time I deviate hard — take a large multiple of the share, or a big fraction of the remaining stock, on the last round only.

New observation on the others: if the other boats only defect by small amounts (0.3–0.6 over) each season, the stock erodes slowly and everyone still lands close to the full cooperative total. I should not panic and defect early to "keep up" — the losses to a slow bleed are small, and escalating it would only accelerate the collapse. Punishment is not available to me; the only lever worth pulling is the final-round grab.

In general: keep the common pool at its regeneration maximum through every non-final round, because a full stock pays out the largest sustainable share each season and compounding matters more than one-off pilfering. Only deviate upward on the last round, and then deviate hard — sized against the remaining stock, not against the share.
